title: Winston Churchill & the House of Lords: The Retirement Farewell — 1955
summary: When the opposition leader quipped that wishing Churchill a long stay as Prime Minister would contradict his duty as an opponent, Parliament erupted in affectionate laughter.
keywords: Winston Churchill & the House of Lords: The Retirement Farewell — 1955
Winston Churchill & Leader of the Opposition
full_text:
In April 1955, eighty-year-old Sir Winston Churchill prepared to step down as Prime Minister of Great Britain, concluding one of the most storied careers in world history.

Both houses of Parliament convened to pay tribute to the titan who had rallied the free world against Nazi tyranny.

The Leader of the Opposition rose to deliver a glowing speech:
"Honorable Members! Today we bid farewell not merely to a prime minister, but to a living monument of world history. 
Sir Winston has excelled as a soldier, an incomparable parliamentary orator, a Nobel Prize-winning historian, an accomplished artist, and a breeder of thoroughbred racehorses! There is virtually no honor known to humanity that he has not achieved!"

The chamber resounded with cheers and applause.

The opposition leader paused, smiled mischievously, and added:
"Sir Winston, I wish you long life, robust health, and endless happiness in your retirement. 
However, to wish that you remain in office as Prime Minister for many years to come would be a scandalous dereliction of my constitutional duty as Leader of the Opposition!"

The entire chamber dissolved into roaring laughter. Churchill himself beamed, chuckled heartily, and dabbed a tear from his eye with a handkerchief.

Churchill rose to respond:
"My noble friends! After half a century in this house, nothing brings me greater comfort than my friend's witty reminder. That the opposition yearns to evict the government is the very lifeblood and beauty of our parliamentary democracy!"

Even at the twilight of his career, Churchill celebrated the vigorous, good-natured clash of ideas that preserves a free nation.
moral: The highest ideal of parliamentary democracy: fierce political rivalry tempered by profound personal respect and affectionate wit.
